solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Critical part on End of Empire

indicators.note: the end of a word is its closing letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: to part is to cut off or separate
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: A historian points to the decisive phase at the close of an empire.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'on' puts the second piece beneath the first; the capitals on 'End' and 'Empire' dress it up as a history title.
explanation.definitionFit: A critical illness or setback is a grave, serious one, so the two adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Dog biting British boys freaking out teenage American girl

indicators.note: something freaking out loses its composure, so these letters lose their order
a mouth that bites closes around what it grips, so the outer word encloses the rest

blocks.note: B is the standard abbreviation for British
taken as written, then rearranged
a boxer is a breed of dog

explanation.surface: A dog snaps at some lads in a frenzy, leaving a girl from the States startled.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog splits after its first two letters to take in the abbreviation and the jumbled boys.
explanation.definitionFit: Bobby-soxer is 1940s American slang for a teenage girl, named for the ankle socks fans of crooners wore.

clue.text: Courts incredibly wise, stopping barbarian

indicators.note: something incredible is beyond belief or normal shape, so the letters are wildly rearranged
to stop a gap is to plug it, so these letters sit inside another word

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the Goths were a Germanic people the Romans called barbarians

explanation.surface: A judge's wisdom halts a savage invader in the law courts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courts' reads as a noun, law courts, but it is the verb: to woo someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who goes with a partner is dating them, which is what courting means as a verb.

clue.text: This Babylonian god, one making Montezuma mad?

indicators.note: a mad arrangement is a crazed, disordered one, so the letters are jumbled
this plus another word making up a whole means the whole minus that word leaves this

blocks.note: the Aztec emperor's name taken as written
taken as written, the part to remove

explanation.surface: A playful question: is this foreign deity the one who drove an Aztec ruler insane?
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus ONE, jumbled, makes MONTEZUMA, so remove ONE from that name's letters and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Tammuz was the Mesopotamian deity of shepherds and vegetation, whose death and return marked the seasons.

clue.text: Exam’s start time clear

indicators.note: only the opening stretch is wanted, so the word loses its tail

blocks.note: a quiz is a short test
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: The time at which an exam begins is made perfectly plain to the candidates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exam's start' tempts you to take a single opening letter; here the start is everything but the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Quit can be an adjective meaning free or rid, as in being well quit of a nuisance, so it means clear.

clue.text: Blimey! Finally uplifted, picked up beauties – wicked women

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting the closing letters upward runs them the other way
to pick up a signal is to hear it, so the sound is what counts

blocks.note: both are exclamations of surprise
belles are beauties; a bel is a unit of loudness

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims as they finally pick up a couple of attractive women, who turn out to be trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the last two letters of the exclamation flip. Blimey is a British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Jezebel, the scheming queen in the Bible, gives her name to any shameless or immoral woman.

clue.text: From yonks ago, Zoom ice lollies at last recollected

indicators.note: at last means at the very end, so only the closing letter is kept
re-collected means gathered up again, so the letters are reassembled in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone fondly remembers a Zoom ice lolly from their childhood.
explanation.walkthrough: Zoom was a rocket-shaped ice lolly sold in Britain; an ice lolly is a popsicle. 'Yonks' is British slang for a very long time.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mesozoic is the geological era of the dinosaurs, so anything from it dates to an extremely remote period.

clue.text: Order warning sign that shows race is over

blocks.note: a cheque is an order to a bank to pay money
a red flag is a signal of danger

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a signal that tells drivers a race has finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order warning sign' reads as an instruction; 'Order' is instead a noun, the bank order. Cheque is the British spelling of check.
explanation.definitionFit: In motor racing the black-and-white chequered flag is waved as the winner crosses the line, ending the race.

clue.text: Charm United, entering uncapped settlement

indicators.note: a cap sits on top, so without it the word loses its first letter
to enter is to go inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a hamlet is a small village
U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names

explanation.surface: A football club moves into a village and wins over the locals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charm' looks like a verb with United as its subject; it is the noun, a lucky trinket.
explanation.definitionFit: An amulet is a small object worn to ward off evil, the same thing as a lucky charm.

clue.text: For example, have brief note returned

indicators.note: a brief version is cut short, so the word loses its final letter
something returned comes back the way it went, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a breve is a long musical note, worth two semibreves

explanation.surface: A message comes back with a short reply, giving an example of possession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have' looks like an instruction to take the note; it is the specimen word being classified.
explanation.definitionFit: Have is a typical example of a doing or being word in grammar, so it illustrates the category.

clue.text: Pressure held in check by second dam, but not the first?

indicators.note: something held in is enclosed, so it sits inside another word

blocks.note: to stem a flow is to check it
P is the symbol for pressure
a second option is the other one

explanation.surface: Water pressure is held back by a second dam in an engineering project.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface dam holds water back; 'dam' is also an animal's mother, and one who is not the first is a later stepparent.
explanation.definitionFit: A dam is a mother, especially of livestock; a mother who was not the original is a stepparent by marriage.

clue.text: Kites flying on bow of junk that skims the water?

indicators.note: things flying about are scattered every which way, so the letters are rearranged
the bow is the front of a boat, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Kites flutter at the prow of a Chinese sailing boat gliding across the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: A junk is a Chinese sailing ship, which fits the watery picture; here only its first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A jet ski is a small motorised craft ridden across the surface of the sea at speed.

clue.text: Opened up end that’s free, finding nothing inside

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order and can rearrange
inside means within, so one piece sits in the middle of another

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
zip is American slang for nothing

explanation.surface: Someone opens a bag at the loose end only to discover it is empty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opened up' looks like the definition, but 'up' belongs to the fodder with 'end'.
explanation.definitionFit: Unzipped means unfastened by pulling down the zip, so a jacket or bag has been opened.

clue.text: Die outside, say, reversing in alley

indicators.note: reversing runs backwards, so the letters go the other way
outside means surrounding, so one phrase wraps another

blocks.note: to pass away is to die
e.g. stands for 'for example', which 'say' also means

explanation.surface: A driver comes to grief backing their car out of a narrow lane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' as 'for example' is a common crossword route to EG.
explanation.definitionFit: An alley is a narrow lane between buildings, which is exactly what a passageway is.

clue.text: Breaking this – as experts, they should sort it out

indicators.note: something broken falls to pieces, so the letters come apart and regroup

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the dash

explanation.surface: Someone says that if a thing gets broken, specialists ought to fix it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' in the surface is a vague thing; in the definition 'it' is the coy euphemism for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Counsellors who treat couples' intimate difficulties are expected to resolve problems in the bedroom.

clue.text: Type of plant in small ditch endlessly blocking stuff up

indicators.note: without ends at either side, so both outer letters go
in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards
a block sits in the way, so it lies inside the other word

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
to stuff a bag is to pack it
a gully is a channel or ditch cut by water

explanation.surface: A gardener finds a plant growing in a little ditch, clogging it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small ditch' wants to be one idea; 'small' stands apart as the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Skullcap is a herb of the mint family, named for its helmet-shaped flowers.

clue.text: Knock over Guinness, oddly enough, getting drinks

indicators.note: the odd positions, first, third, fifth and so on, are the ones kept

blocks.note: an engine pinks when it knocks from premature ignition
the letters in odd positions

explanation.surface: Someone spills a pint of stout and, strangely, ends up with a round of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'over' puts the first piece above the second. Guinness is an Irish stout.
explanation.definitionFit: Pink gin is gin flavoured with Angostura bitters, a classic naval cocktail, so these are drinks.

clue.text: Dug into endless dispute involving single daughter

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is dropped
to involve is to include, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a quarrel is an argument
I is the Roman numeral one
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A parent gets drawn into a long-running row with an only daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dug into' reads as one phrase; 'Dug' alone is the definition and 'into' just links it.
explanation.definitionFit: To quarry is to extract stone from the ground by excavation, so quarried is a past tense of digging.

clue.text: Upset AC/DC partners, formerly lofty, horny types?

indicators.note: upset means turned upside down, which in a down entry runs letters backwards

blocks.note: AC/DC is slang for bisexual, shortened to bi
former partners are exes

explanation.surface: Former lovers, upset and once high-minded, turn out to be randy sorts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horny' looks like slang for lustful, and the AC/DC slang supports that; it means having horns, and 'lofty' points to mountain heights.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibexes are wild mountain goats with large curving horns that live high on Alpine crags.

clue.text: Tidy little number worn away

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for number
eaten away means worn away

explanation.surface: A neat little outfit has been worn until it frays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tidy little number' reads like a smart dress; 'little' signals the shortened form of number.
explanation.definitionFit: To tidy something is to make it orderly, the same verb as making it neat.

clue.text: Panacea made by character abroad cutting nettle up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading bottom to top, so the letters run backwards
a cut goes into something, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: to nettle is to irritate or rile
xi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A cure-all is concocted by a foreign herbalist chopping up stinging nettles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nettle' suggests a herbal ingredient; it is the verb meaning irritate. A character abroad is a foreign alphabet letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An elixir is a supposed remedy for every ailment, which is exactly what a panacea is.

clue.text: Artful hag felt moved to demonstrate support

indicators.note: things moved are shifted into new places, so the letters change order

blocks.note: fly is British slang for sharp or crafty
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A cunning old witch was stirred to show her backing for a cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artful' looks like an adjective for the hag; it stands alone as the slang word for crafty.
explanation.definitionFit: To fly the flag is an idiom for publicly championing one's country or cause, so it means showing backing.

clue.text: Observe branch

blocks.note: first meaning: British informal verb, to notice or realise
second meaning: a small shoot of a tree

explanation.walkthrough: 'Observe branch' sounds like an instruction to look at a tree; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To twig is British slang for catching on or noticing, and a twig is a slender shoot off a bough.

clue.text: Unlimited bogies, very disagreeable

indicators.note: without limits at either side, so both outer letters go

blocks.note: bogies are goblins or bogeymen, wicked spirits

explanation.surface: Endless nasty bogeys, very unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: A bogie, as in bogeyman, is a goblin or evil spirit, not the railway or golf senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Evil can mean extremely unpleasant, as with an evil smell or temper, beyond its moral sense.

clue.text: A woman in church on new year’s day

indicators.note: in an across entry, being on something means following it, so this piece is placed second

blocks.note: New Year's Day is the first of January, Jan 1, with I as the Roman one
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A woman attends a church service on the first day of January.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' places the church after the date in an across entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Janice is a female given name, so it fits a woman in general.

clue.text: Shoot half a what-d’you-call it into Kipling’s better man?

indicators.note: only half the word is wanted, so its second half is dropped

blocks.note: to shoot is to gun down
a gadget is a thingamajig, a device whose name escapes you
into indicates going in

explanation.surface: Someone fires part of an unnamed contraption at the hero of a famous poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's poem ends 'You're a better man than I am, Gunga Din', praising an Indian water-carrier.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's narrator, a British soldier, declares the water-bearer the better man, so the title figure is meant.
